Introduction - December 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

Base metal prices have retreated from their elevated highs seen in mid November.  The GFMS Base Metal price index is down to 333 on December 6 from its November 11 peak of 356.  Part of this reflects the recent rebound of the US dollar, but also prices have attracted some profit-taking following the exceptional price performance seen in recent months. The key feature in our view for 2011 is the extent to which the individual base metals will be able to cling onto th

e gains achieved in 2010 rather than necessarily posting strong increases (see individual sections for price projections for 2011). 

Base metal prices benefited this year this from the sharp rebound in demand from the mature economies.  2010 stands out in that the bulk of the demand growth was from this region rather than from the emerging economies.  In 2011, GFMS expects that the focus will once again shift back to the emerging economies and that growth in the mature economies will revert back towards trend, which essentially means little or no year-on-year growth from this source in 2011. 

Other aspects of the market fundamentals look more positive.  The bulk of the data pertaining to China remains bullish for the LME-traded metals. As detailed later in this report the economic data –industrial production growth, fixed asset investment and the latest purchasing managers’ index – all point to sustained growth.  On the supply side, we note that production of primary aluminium output has been cut back sharply.  Output growth for both lead and zinc within China has also slowed.  The demand data for other emerging regions such as the ASEAN countries, India and Brazil remain encouraging with these countries posting strong year-onyear gains.   However in terms of price forecasts, GFMS tends to view 2011 as a period of consolidation rather than significant gains from the levels seen in early December. 

Copper prices have recently set new all-time highs in excess of $9,000/tonne.  GFMS has just published its latest Quarterly Three year Copper Forecast, which gives our views on the market balance and price out to 2013.  In order to receive a copy of the Executive Summary of this report, please contact: 

###### **Charles.demeester@gfms.co.uk** , or 

###### **Carmen.eleta@gfms.co.uk** 

Prices for copper, in particular, have been supported by the likely launch of physically-backed ETFs on base metals.  It appears that much of the buying seen in early December is associated with the pending launch of a copper-based fund.  For copper, this purchasing is obviously imposed on an already tight physical market.  Although this has supported the copper price, we harbour doubts about the launch of these funds given that the costs to investors are still far from clear. 

Apart from the ETFs, the most positive factor is the limited supply response to higher prices.  The most notable example is that of aluminium.  Efforts by Chinese authorities to curb energy consumption to meet targets set for the current 5-year planning period, in advance of the latter finishing at the end of the year, have led to a significant reduction in output.  As we discuss in detail in the relevant section of this Base Metals One Year Forecast, this has led us to adjust our projections for the final quarter of this year and the first three months of 2011 to show an essentially balanced market.  For a number of the other base metals, most notably copper and tin, the supply shortfall is m

ore structural in its nature. As a result, we are only seeing limited gains to output despite the high level of prices. Base Metals & Other Commodity Prices

The index rose to a noticeable 36-month high to 105.3. While the improvement is encouraging, sentiment will be tested as we move into 2011 by ongoing concerns over the sustainability of the recovery and European sovereign debt problems. Recent statistics from Japan, however, have been far less encouraging for the base metals sector. Industrial production notably declined for a fifth consecutive month, dipping by almost 2.0% month-on-month in October. The year-on-year figure although remained in positive territory slowed to 6.1% as opposed to near 30% in March. Weakening exports and sluggish domestic demand have both seen production fall sharply in recent months. Japan’s housing starts in October also came in weaker than expected. Starts, which increased by 6.4% year-on-year, slowed considerably from the impressive 17.7% and 20.5% growth registered in September and August, respectively. Although ongoing government measures to support homebuying and slightly better credit availability are expected to provide some support in the coming months, a weak labour market combined with persistent deflation and the recent dip in consumer confidence will undoubtedly limit any gains. |||**~~Ma~~**|**~~in Econo~~

However, it should be remembered that while the increase is positive, confidence remains weak and is not supporting spending. Manufacturing in the country has been holding up well. Although the Institute for Supply Management’s manufacturing index (ISM) edged slightly lower in November from October’s 56.9 to 56.6, the index remained above its third quarter average, providing further evidence that the recovery has re-accelerated. The US auto industry is also faring better. Vehicle sales in November equalled to those in October, coming in at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate of 12.25 million units. Other than August 2009, when cash for clunkers pumped up sales, this is the highest level since September 2008. The slightly stronger pace in recent months is occurring as pentup demand built up during the recession is released. Conditions in China remain upbeat. Despite having been moderating since the start of the year, fixed asset investment growth remained impressive in October, especially when considering an extremely high base last year. The Chinese manufacturing sectors has been strengthening in recent months, signalled by the country’s PMI, which rose to 55.3 in November from 54.6 in the previous month. the first time the “red metal” has traded above $9,000/tonne in the contract’s history. Dollar weakness, and more recently technical trading, have been the major factors behind this rally._** - **_A record 32-day strike at Xstrata and Anglo American’s Collahuasi mine finally came to a conclusion on 7th December. The material effect of the walkout on the market is however believed to have been limited by the use of non-union and temporary workers and a previous stockpiling of material._** - **_LME inventories have continued to fall over the month and, on the Shanghai Futures Exchange, stocks have begun to reverse the gains seen up to mid-November. Tightness has reportedly been added as a result of a dominant warrant holder controlling 50-80% of LME warrants since late November, with the cash-to-threes backwardation subsequently widening._** - **_GFMS continue to forecast a correction in copper prices over the first half of 2011, in light of our expectations for a slow-down in global economic growth. Importantly, with current prices well in excess of marginal production costs, the supply response to such developments would be limited. Consequently, with the market returning to a surplus position over the first and second quarters, GFMS expect to see a correction well below the $8,000/ tonne level._** - **_Thereafter, investors are expected to return towards copper as consumption accelerates over the second half. Intensified by the structural supply constraints, copper is forecast to record a full year deficit of 132,000 tonnes over 2011, almost double that expected for this year._** - **_These factors will culminate in a progressive strengthening of prices over the second half of 2011, rising to a peak of close to $10,000/ tonne by year-end. This will support a full-year average of $8,175/tonne._** ###### **Outlook for the next 12 months** ###### **~~GFMS’ Forecast Scenarios~~** - **_GFMS have revised upwards our projections for mature economy demand over the fourth quarter. This has served to widen the projected deficit to 68,000 tonnes for the year as a whole. Source: GFMS Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - December 2010 ###### **Market background** Copper prices have risen to a new record high on a cash official basis on 7th December of $9,024/tonne on technical buying and a weakening dollar, in part resulting from a marginal easing of concerns over the euro zone debt crisis. Another potential contributor to the recent rally has been the revelation that a single trader is holding between 50-80% of copper cash warrants on the LME. This has served to perpetuate the market tightness that we have consistently noted, and is believed to be a key reason behind the cashto-threes premium rising to a peak of $89 on an official basis in late November, representing the largest backwardation since October 2008. Prices had previously shown volatile performance over November. Price strength was seen earlier in the month when official cash prices reached $8,925/tonne on 11th November, and the metal even breached the all-time-high on an intra-day basis, on a weaker dollar and positive Chinese data. Upward momentum was also supported by a strike over pay at the Collahuasi mine which, although the dispute has now been resolved, has served as a reminder of the supply-side problems which continue to hang over the market. Following this, and prior to the recent rally, prices experienced a correction back towards $8,150/tonne on concerns over the global economic outlook. Total exchange stocks continued their uptrend over the first half of November, after rising for the first time since April during the previous month, due to an increase in inventories on the Shanghai Futures Exchange to a recent high of 126,736 tonnes in the middle of the month. The increase in total exchange stocks took place despite LME inventories continuing their downtrend, albeit at a slower pace than previously, ending the month at 354,850 tonnes. More recent movements have been more reflective of the current tight conditions in the market, with SHFE inventories falling by almost 10,000 tonnes from their mid-November peak. ###### **~~Weekly Change in LME stocks vs Spot Price~~** 500 8800

The outlook has been further clouded by a 32-day strike at Xstrata and Anglo American’s Collahuasi mine following failed wage talks early last month. Output at the mine has undoubtedly been affected over the course of the strike period, although the loss is thought to have been in part contained by the use of non-union and temporary workers, and a previous stockpiling of material, which allowed the mine to continue shipments of material to European and Asian buyers. Elsewhere in Chile, pay deals have been struck at Antofagasta’s Los Pelambres and Codelco’s Radomiro Tomic mines, averting concerns that developments at Collahuasi could result in a flurry of stoppages at a time when copper prices are at record highs. (CNMC) has announced that it is to suspend operations at its Baluba copper mine for 45 days, starting on 15th November, to replace its ore hoisting system. As noted in our previous Base Metals One Year Forecast, African production has been growing strongly, with the latest data from the Zambian Central Bank showing a 21% year-on-year rise in copper concentrate production over the first nine months of the year to over 625,000 tonnes. Elsewhere, Aurubis has noted that all copper concentrate processing operations at its main works in Hamburg have been halted as a result of an accident which occurred on the opening days of

the month. It is believed that repairs could take around two weeks to complete, with copper anodes needing to be sourced from other locations during this period to allow production of cathode and copper products to continue largely unaffected. Despite the projected concentrate shortage next year, smelters in Japan and China are pushing for higher term treatment and refining charges (TC/RC’s) over 2011. Spot TC/RC’s have been on the increase of late, in part a result of the suspension of Sterlite Industries’ Tuticorin smelter/ refinery as mentioned in previous reports. Having said this, the uptick must be placed into the context of the very low base. ###### **Chinese consumption continues to slow into fourth quarter** The downtrend in Chinese copper semis production, our preferred indicator of underlying copper demand in the country, continued in October, with the 837,000 tonne total falling marginally from the previous month. This decline was in part due to the swathe of power limitations imposed by local governments over the fourth quarter in particular, which affected operations at processing plants. The October total was nevertheless up on a year-on-year basis although, partly in line with a higher base effect, represented a slow down from the rates seen earlier in the year. Cumulative semis output rose 13.6% to 8.090 million tonnes over the first ten months. The recent slowdown in demand has been reflected in the country’s import numbers, with inflows of refined metal falling nearly 30% month-on-month in October to 169,871 tonnes, the lowest level seen since October of last year. In addition to the aforementioned slowing of real demand in line with seasonal factors, imports of refined metal have also been somewhat distorted by high LME prices, discouraging imports of material. On a similar theme, inflows of scrap, used as a substitute to refined metal, also fell by a significant 23% over the month. Going forward, anecdotal evidence has suggested that, following a sell-off of stocks over the start of the final quarter, scrap availability is once again beginning to tighten, pushing up scrap prices, which could help support demand for refined metal over the close of the year. GFMS expect Chinese consumption to rise by 9.0% this year. Despite this growth slowing to 7.0% over 2011, this would still represent a significant increase in tonnage terms. Our optimism on continued Chinese growth is supported by ongoing investment in the national grid as detailed under the latest 5 year plan running from 2011-2015. LME Stocks vs Spot Price

Independent - Informed - International **C3** Copper - December 2010 ###### **Mature economy demand growth set to slow but rising premiums reflect projected tightness on supply concerns** Following a stronger than expected recovery in demand in the mature economies over 2010, GFMS are expecting a slowdown in the rate of growth of copper consumption next year. There have indeed been signs of this materialising in Japan over the final months of the year, with manufacturers not being helped by a stronger yen. Indeed, Japanese copper wire and cable shipments fell 2.1% month-on-month and 3.9% year-on-year in October and rolled copper product output growth also slowed 3.3% on a month-on-month basis, although remained up when compared with October 2009. Despite a slowing of mature economy growth next year, the market is braced for growing market tightness in the face of lacklustre supply growth. Indicative of this, Codelco is reportedly looking to increase annual physical copper premiums to buyers in Japan and South Korea by 31% next year to $98, from $75 in 2010. It is also pressing for higher premiums from Chinese buyers, in the region of $115, up around 35% on those seen this year. ###### **Market outlook** Since the previous edition of our Base Metals One Year Forecast, GFMS has undertaken a revision of our medium term projections for the recently published November edition of our Quarterly Three Year Copper Forecast. Highlighting the metal’s weak fundamentals, LME stocks have continued to trend upwards. Inventories on the exchange have notably risen to levels last seen in mid-June. However, the total stock accumulation over November which came in at almost 3,650 tonnes was 20% lower from the previous month. ###### **Global demand growth decelerates over JanuarySeptember** According to the latest data by the World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), global nickel consumption, which totalled 1.12 million tonnes, continued to post above 10% year-onyear growth up to September, a trend that has been in place since the start of the year. However, the increase which came in at +11.9% was somewhat lower than the growth observed over the first eight months (+15.5%). Notably, the mature economies – which we term as Europe, Japan and the United States – have continued to register strong growth, with demand in the region up by more than 40% year-on-year over January-September as a whole. Within this group, consumption in the United States grew by the largest rate (+52.7%). This is somewhat surprising particularly as the underlying economy has been weakening, as reflected in the month-on-month figures. Nevertheless, such high growth is largely the result of an extremely low 2009 base. Although the other two economies also grew robustly, experiencing nickel demand growth of +47.2% and +26.1%, respectively, it is clear that demand in both Europe and Japan is also easing from levels seen over the first half of the year. According to the latest statistics from the ISSF, stainless output in Europe rose by around 50% in the first half of this year. Stainless output in Asia (excluding China) registered a 40% advance in this period. ###### **Nickel premiums continue to drop on Vale’s Sudbury restart** Physical premiums, which provide a good indication of whe

re demand stands, have continued to fall, as market participants focus on concluding negotiations for 2011 amid continued pressure from the increased availability of material due to the restart of Vale’s Sudbury operations and to some extent lower demand from stainless steel mills. Nickel premiums for melting-grade material are at 35-50 cents/lb down by 29% from the previous range of 50-70 cents/lb, while plating-grade premiums have declined by 17.5% from a previous range of $0.90-1.10/lb to $0.65-1.0/lb. Premiums are likely to remain under pressure as consumers will stay out of the market until contract negotiations are completed. Nickel Premiums

###### **Chinese imports rise by a fifth in October as Norilsk uses a faster route** The China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association (CNI-A) has recently released its trade statistics. Chinese imports of refined nickel jumped by more than 20% month-on-month in October to 19,045 tonnes, helped by a surge in imports from Russia after Norilsk Nickel began using a new Arctic sea route to Asia. Shipments from Russia were 12,352 tonnes, up 40.5% on September. Importantly, the new route cut delivery times from Russia to Asian markets by as much as two thirds. ###### **Mine production is picking up** We continue to note further advances on the supply-side. In terms of mine output, Xstrata will restart production at the suspended Sinclair mine “in the near future” as nickel prices remain largely upbeat, as opposed to when the mine closed down. The mine will produce 6,000 tonnes of nickel in concentrate per year. Similarly, Norilsk Nickel has reopened an operation at the Nkomati mine in South Africa earlier than expected. It is believed that the Nkomati mine will produce 12,300 tonnes of nickel-in-concentrate this year. Also, Talvivaara Mining continued to ramp up production at its Sotkamo mine in Eastern Finland in the third quarter, despite the technical challenges encountered earlier in the year. This saw its nickel production rise by 18% compared with the previous quarter. As such, total output for the first nine months came in at 6,550 tonnes. The company believes that it will achieve its 30,000 tonne production target by year-end, which follows a previous downgrade due to delays as mentioned above. The Sotkamo resource expansion has demonstrated the potential to exceed the next production target of 50,000 tonnes by 2012. ###### **New Caledonian output set to surge** Societe Le Nickel (SLN) has recently unveiled plans to boost output by almost 20% in the next three years. Significant increases were registered at the Katanga operation in the DRC and Votorantim in Brazil. The bottom line is an increase in production of close to 50% in the first six months of the year. Although we believe that the Chinese figure may overstate the increase, it is clear that the market has had to absorb a lot of extra metal. ###### **…with further increases in the pipeline** The cobalt market will also have to absorb higher output associated with the growth in refined nickel production reflecting higher utilization rates at existing operations and new capacity. Production should rise sharply at Vale following the resolution of the strike at Sudbury. It appears that the strike at the company’s Voisey’s Bay operation is finally reaching its conclusion. Vale is also in the process of ramping up its Goro project that could eventually yield 4,000 tpy of cobalt. Other contributors to extra cobalt production in 2011 should include Sherritt Gordon’s 5,600 tpy Ambatovy project. The market will also have to absorb projects from the African cobalt-belt the largest of which is Tenke. ###### **Market and price outlook** Although we remain positive about the demand prospects for cobalt, the market is having to cope with a surge in supply. The increase to supply is coming from a variety of sources – the reactivation of capacity hit by strikes, the expansion to existing capacity and, most notably, a large number of greenfield projects. The new capacity is coming from a large number of projects and they are being developed by mainstream nickel-cobalt producers. As such, we are not expecting a repeat of the problems associated with the first generation of high pressure acid leach operations, when actual production was massively below expectations. Therefore we continue to forecast that the market will be in a surplus in 2011. |**~~Quarterly Cobalt Supply-Demand Balance - Base Case~~**| |---| |(000 tonnes)|**2010**
